drapeaux.note: The phrase “the only courtroom door remaining open to evidence secured by official lawlessness” is copied verbatim from Part III of Justice Clark's opinion in Mapp v. Ohio, 367 U.S. 643 (1961), as published at https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/367/643 (checked on a mirror copy of the opinion, since the Cornell page itself could not be opened).

The French puts « la seule porte du prétoire encore ouverte » in quotation marks and says that leaving the possibility open amounts to keeping that door open. In the opinion the phrase is about closing it: the Court says it is led to “close the only courtroom door remaining open to evidence secured by official lawlessness.” The sense is close, but the quoted fragment is framed as if the Court spoke of keeping the door open. To be checked by controler/reparer.

titre: A warrantless search changed what evidence proves
accroche: Cleveland, 1957: police search a house without a valid warrant. In 1961, the Supreme Court draws a rule from it that reaches far beyond this case.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1957, Cleveland police come to Dollree Mapp's home: they are looking for Virgil Ogletree, a suspect in a bombing case, and suspect that gambling paraphernalia tied to Mapp's companion is on the premises. Mapp refuses to let them in without a warrant. Three hours later, several officers come back and force their way in. She demands to see the warrant; a piece of paper is held up, which she grabs and tucks into her bosom after a brief scuffle. The officers handcuff her and search the whole house. No warrant will ever be produced at trial. The search does turn up Ogletree, hiding in the downstairs tenant's apartment (he will later be cleared in the bombing investigation), as well as betting slips, a charge of which Mapp herself will be acquitted. But it is materials judged obscene, found at the same time, which Ohio law forbids possessing, that bring Mapp her conviction.

## A rule that already existed, but not everywhere

Since 1914, the Supreme Court has barred federal courts from using evidence obtained through an illegal search: this is the exclusionary rule. But in 1949, in *Wolf v. Colorado*, the same Court had held that this rule did not bind the states: a state could recognize the right to a lawful search without throwing out the evidence gathered in violating it. The evidence was still unlawfully obtained, but usable.

## What the June 19, 1961 ruling changes

In an opinion by Justice Tom Clark, the Supreme Court overrules *Wolf*. It holds that the protection against arbitrary searches, guaranteed by the Fourth Amendment and made binding on the states by the Fourteenth, would remain a right without a sanction if evidence obtained in violating it could still be used to convict. The Court writes that, by overruling *Wolf*, it closes “the only courtroom door remaining open to evidence secured by official lawlessness.” All evidence gathered in violation of the Constitution thus becomes inadmissible in state courts, as it already was in federal courts.

## The shift

The case originally involves neither a murder nor a contested piece of technical evidence: a handful of publications found without a warrant produce a rule that has shaped the work of American police ever since. *Mapp v. Ohio* does not say that an unlawful search has no consequences for the officers who carried it out: it says it must have one at trial itself, by stripping the prosecution of the use of what it obtained that way. The most solid evidence, obtained outside the rules, stops being evidence in front of the judge.

repere.texte: On June 19, 1961, in Mapp v. Ohio, the U.S. Supreme Court holds that all evidence obtained through a search that violates the Constitution is inadmissible in state courts, overruling its own 1949 precedent, Wolf v. Colorado.
repere.source: Mapp v. Ohio, 367 U.S. 643 (1961), U.S. Supreme Court, opinion of Justice Clark

carte.punch: A warrant never shown changed what a court can hold against you
carte.idee: In 1957, Cleveland police search a house without ever producing a warrant. In 1961, the Supreme Court holds that evidence obtained through an illegal search becomes unusable in any American court, federal or state.
carte.source_courte: Mapp v. Ohio, U.S. Supreme Court, 1961

quiz.question: What does Mapp v. Ohio (1961) change compared with the situation left by Wolf v. Colorado (1949)?
choix: It creates, for the first time, a right to be protected against warrantless searches
It makes all evidence obtained through an illegal search inadmissible in state courts
It removes the police's obligation to get a warrant before any search of a home
It gives federal courts alone jurisdiction over cases of unlawful searches
quiz.explication: Before 1961, Wolf v. Colorado recognized the right to a lawful search without requiring state courts to throw out evidence obtained in violating it. Mapp v. Ohio extends to the states the exclusionary rule already applied in federal courts since 1914.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what basis is Dollree Mapp convicted, according to the entry?
choix: On possession of gambling paraphernalia, found during the search of her home
On materials judged obscene, found during a search for which no warrant was produced at trial
On her initial refusal to let the police in, treated as obstruction of law enforcement
On her alleged part in the bombing that the police had come to her home to investigate
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The search does turn up the suspect being sought and gambling materials, but Mapp is acquitted of that charge, tied to her companion; she is convicted only of possessing materials judged obscene, found at the same time, while no warrant was produced at trial.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Since when did the exclusionary rule already apply to federal courts before Mapp v. Ohio?
choix: Since 1991, following a federal reform of criminal procedure
Since 1914, under an earlier Supreme Court precedent
Since the ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment, in 1868
Since 1961, with Mapp v. Ohio creating the rule for the first time
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The exclusionary rule already existed for federal courts since 1914. What Mapp v. Ohio changes in 1961 is its extension to state courts, which had not been bound by it since Wolf v. Colorado (1949).
